name: Dar Fur Daju
confidence_why: Dimmendaal (2015), from his own Lagowa field data, describes one high pitch peak per word whose position is lexically unpredictable and explicitly rejects the stress analysis of Ismail (2007) for the same variety, while Tucker and Bryan (1966) record three tone levels alongside an uninvestigated role for stress, so the prosodic type of Dar Fur Daju is openly contested in print and no source states a stress-placement rule.

sweep_summary: darf1239 (Dar Fur Daju; Lagawa/Lagowa and Nyala are Glottolog alternate names) is not in the catalog. The only titled item, Ismail 2007 'Noun Classes in Daju Lagawa and the Role of Stress' (Köppe, Nilo-Saharan 22: 115-122), is about this language (Glottolog links it to [daj]) but could not be opened: no open copy anywhere reachable, publisher PDF for purchase, Harvard print (Widener Library (offsite storage) PL8026.N49 N54 2001) -> HIGH priority to acquire. Second-hand, the JALL 30 (2009: 107) review calls it a number-marking taxonomy, and Dimmendaal 2015 (The Leopard's Spots, ch. 3, pp. 32-33; Brill, paywalled) reports from his own unpublished data that Nuba-Mountains Daju 'appear to have tonal accent' with 'one prominent high peak (involving pitch rather than intensity) per word in most cases', explicitly disputing Ismail's stress claim; Alamin Mubarak 2006/2013a's stress analysis concerns Laggori (a different Daju language). Both Ismail 2007 and Dimmendaal 2015 pp. 32-33 are the pages to get; neither snippet gives a placement rule. On-disk material (Aviles 2008: initial stress in Dar Daju Daju of Chad, dard1243; Boyeldieu 2009: Lagowa data unmarked for tone/stress) does not describe darf1239 stress. Google/Bing/DDG/Mojeek/Brave, Brill, SIL, HathiTrust, archive. Saved: ( updated).

new_statements.quote: Daju languages spoken in the Nuba Mountains appear to have tonal accent (as do Cushitic languages like Somali). Ismail (2007) argues that there is stress in Daju of Lagowa, a claim that does not tally with my own unpublished data. According to my data, there appears to be one prominent high peak (involving pitch rather than intensity) per word in most cases.

new_statements.reading: First-hand (own field data) but snippet-level: Lagowa Daju (darf1239) is claimed to have a pitch accent/tonal-accent system with one prominent high pitch peak per word, contradicting Ismail 2007's stress analysis; the position of the peak is not stated in the recovered text, and the author himself flags the analysis as needing a proper phonetic study. Not a stress-placement statement; it is a prosodic-type statement (pitch accent, not intensity stress) that any future catalog's classification for darf1239 must weigh against Ismail 2007 pp. 115-122.

new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's Daju chapter covers the whole Daju group ('Eastern: SHATT and LIGURI; Western: DAJU and NJALGULGULE') and draws most examples from Stevenson's Shatt (eastern) material; the western 'DAJU' (Sila/Nyala/Lagowa) subsumes darf1239 but the tone-and-stress sentence is not variety-specific. Dimmendaal 2015's existing statement is specifically about Daju of Lagowa (darf1239).

tone_statements.quote: The first distinction made in this chapter is between languages with and languages without tones. For most languages it is easy to determine if the language does or does not make use of tone, but there are surprisingly sharp disagreements in certain cases. For example, Dar Fur Daju (Nilo-Saharan; Sudan) is reported as non-tonal in one source but transcribed with three tone levels in another.

readall_conflicts: Tucker & Bryan 1966 (group level, mainly Shatt data) report three tone levels with no lexical tone doublets and an uninvestigated but apparently important stress; Dimmendaal 2015 (own unpublished Lagowa data, snippet-level) describes a tonal/pitch accent system with one prominent high peak per word and explicitly rejects Ismail 2007's stress analysis of Lagowa Daju; Ismail 2007 (not opened, no open copy) argues for stress. None of the three gives a placement rule for darf1239. The disagreement is over prosodic type (tone vs pitch accent vs stress), not placement; Tucker & Bryan's 'no tonal doublets' is at least consistent with Dimmendaal's accentual reading.
